atoms.canonical_statement: The analysis assessed effects of invasive procedures, hemostatic and clinical variables, beta-blocker timing, and rt-PA dose on hemorrhagic events.
TIMI II was a multicenter randomized controlled trial; this report analyzed hemorrhagic outcomes from the trial.
The report included 3339 TIMI II patients enrolled from April 1986 through June 1988.

atoms.canonical_statement: Patients were eligible if they were younger than 76 years, had ischemic chest pain for at least 30 minutes, and could start treatment within 4 hours of symptom onset.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that an invasive management strategy increased morbidity from hemorrhagic complications in acute myocardial infarction patients treated with rt-PA, heparin, and aspirin.
The authors interpreted the 100-mg strategy comparison as a 68% increase in major hemorrhage and a 45% increase in major or minor hemorrhage with invasive management.

The authors noted that some hemoglobin-based hemorrhagic events without an identified site could reflect phlebotomy, laboratory or measurement error, small unobserved blood losses, and rehydration, potentially overestimating bleeding frequency.
The authors cautioned that the association between fibrinogenolysis markers and hemorrhage was too weak for clinical prediction in individual patients.
The authors suggested that the platelet decline occurring after rt-PA completion and during heparin exposure made rt-PA an unlikely primary cause and suggested heparin may have contributed.
The authors stated that interpretation of the 150-mg versus 100-mg rt-PA comparison must consider concurrent changes in TIMI II eligibility criteria and aspirin timing.
The study was supported by National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute research contracts and NHLBI grants HL35058 and HL38460.

extraction_limitations: Language-model extraction has not received human verification; atoms are marked needs_review.

The rt-PA 150-mg and 100-mg cohorts were sequential protocol eras rather than a randomized dose comparison; dose-associated atoms preserve the reported results but should not be read as randomized causal estimates.

The paper reports multiple secondary and exploratory associations; not every descriptive site-level table cell was converted into a separate atom when a more independently useful aggregate assertion captured the result.
PDF text extraction contained occasional glyph/OCR-like substitutions (for example µ and 10^9/L); key table values were reconciled against rendered pages.
